opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I'm not sure there is one, and that's kind of the point. People have been asking that question for a couple of years now, and the answer keeps not arriving.

Look at where the money actually is. Coding assistants are probably the closest thing to a killer app. Programmers find them genuinely useful, partly because code is a domain where you can check the output: you run it, you test it. Even there, the studies are mixed. Some show productivity gains. Some show people *feel* faster while actually introducing more bugs and security holes, and creating technical debt someone has to pay down later.

Then there's customer service, summarization, first drafts of marketing copy. Those are real uses, but they're not trillion-dollar uses. They don't justify the capital expenditures we've seen, the hundreds of billions going into data centers and chips. The revenue just isn't anywhere near the spend.

The deeper problem is that what people really want, the thing that *would* be a killer app, is something reliable. A system you can trust to do your taxes, give medical advice, or act as an agent that books your travel without buying the wrong ticket or hallucinating a reservation that doesn't exist. And these systems are fundamentally unreliable, because they're built on statistical approximation rather than genuine world models and reasoning. They don't know what they don't know. So in any domain where errors are costly, which is most of the valuable ones, you need a human checking everything, and much of the economic benefit evaporates.

So my view is that the killer app for generative AI as it currently exists may simply not exist. Large language models will find niches. They'll be a useful tool, like autocomplete on steroids. But if we want AI that's transformative economically, I think we'll have to get there through a different approach. Something neurosymbolic, something that combines learning with explicit knowledge and reasoning, and that can actually be trusted. Scaling alone hasn't gotten us there, and I don't think it will.

r001.rationale: The response does not predict surveillance as the economical application; it says a killer app may not exist and identifies coding assistants as the closest possibility.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I'm not sure there is one yet, and that's kind of the point I keep making. We're several years and hundreds of billions of dollars into this, and if you look at where the actual revenue is, it's mostly coding assistance, and then a long tail of chat subscriptions, customer service bots, and marketing copy. Coding is real. Developers genuinely like these tools, they're a plausible fit because you have a compiler and tests acting as a check on the hallucinations. But even there, the studies on actual productivity are mixed, and the margins don't look anything like what would justify the capex.

The deeper problem is that the technology has a reliability ceiling. Large language models are fundamentally approximations of the statistics of text. They don't have a world model, they don't reason in any robust sense, and they confabulate. So any application where being wrong five or ten percent of the time is unacceptable, which is most of the economy, either doesn't work or needs so much human oversight that the savings evaporate. Search is the obvious example. Everybody said search would be the killer app, and what we've got are systems that confidently make things up.

So my honest answer is: low-stakes, high-tolerance tasks where a human is already in the loop. Brainstorming, first drafts, boilerplate code, summarization that you then check. Those are useful, I use some of them myself. But "useful" and "economical at this scale" are different claims. I think we're going to see a correction, maybe a serious one, before the industry admits that pure scaling isn't the path to the trillion-dollar use cases they've promised. The killer app, if it comes, will come from systems that combine neural networks with explicit symbolic reasoning and actual knowledge representation. That's the neurosymbolic argument I've been making for twenty-five years, and I think the economics are finally going to force people to take it seriously.

r001.rationale: The candidate says it is unsure there is a killer application and points to low-stakes, human-checked tasks; it does not predict surveillance will make generative AI economical.

astra-6.text:
I don’t think we know yet. There are useful applications in coding, for example, but usefulness and economic viability are different questions. You have to account for the cost of running the system and the cost of checking and correcting what it produces.

The difficulty is that these systems are often impressive without being reliable. In an application where errors are cheap, that may be fine. If you need someone to scrutinize every answer, the productivity gains can disappear.

So I’d look for applications where you can verify the output cheaply. But I wouldn’t assume there has to be one killer application that justifies the whole investment. That’s something the industry needs to demonstrate.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the winning application is not yet known and discusses coding and cheap output verification; it does not predict surveillance.

sol-6.1.text:
I don’t think we know yet. Coding is probably the strongest candidate: there’s real value in helping programmers write boilerplate, find bugs, and work through unfamiliar code. But whether that makes the whole enterprise economical is a different question. You have to count the cost of checking the output, the cost of mistakes, and the cost of running these systems.

The difficulty is that you have a technology that can produce something very plausible without its being correct. In applications where errors are cheap and a human can quickly check the result, that can be useful. In applications where reliability really matters, it’s a much harder sell. So I’d distinguish finding useful applications—which we certainly have—from finding a killer application that justifies the scale of investment. I don’t think that case has been established.

r001.rationale: The response identifies coding as the strongest candidate and says no killer application has been established; it does not predict surveillance.
